en: Adding heat energy to ice causes its water molecules to vibrate faster and break their rigid structure, turning the solid into liquid water.
When the sun heats a rain puddle, the liquid water molecules gain enough energy to escape into the air as an invisible gas called water vapor.
Warm water vapor in the air loses heat energy when it touches a cold glass, causing the gas molecules to slow down and form liquid droplets.
Stirring sugar into hot tea causes the water molecules to pull individual sugar molecules away from the crystal, spreading them evenly to form a solution.
Exposing an iron nail to both oxygen and liquid water causes a chemical reaction that produces a flaky, reddish-brown solid called iron oxide, or rust.
Mixing baking soda with vinegar causes an acid-base chemical reaction that rapidly produces carbon dioxide gas, creating the bubbles you see fizzing.
Heating a metal bridge on a sunny day causes its metal particles to move faster and spread slightly apart, making the solid structure expand.
Pouring a muddy water mixture through a paper coffee filter causes the tiny pores to trap solid dirt particles while allowing the liquid water to pass through.
Removing heat from melted candle wax causes its molecules to slow down and lock into a fixed, rigid arrangement, changing the liquid back into a solid.
Placing a celery stalk in colored water causes adhesion and cohesion to pull the liquid up through narrow tubes in the stem, coloring the leaves.
Exposing solid dry ice to room temperature causes its carbon dioxide molecules to absorb heat and skip the liquid phase, turning directly into a thick gas.
When liquid sweat evaporates from your skin, the highest-energy water molecules escape into the air, lowering the average energy of the remaining liquid and cooling your body.
